_readme: One entry per partner. Edit here, then run `python3 partners/build.py` to regenerate partners/<slug>/index.html and partners/index.html. Empty strings and empty lists are fine: the page simply omits that section. Fields: slug (URL), name, url (their site), tagline (one line), tags (3), cohort (label shown on the page, e.g. '2026 cohort'), term (e.g. '2026–2031'), led_by, serves, offers (list of short items), what (1 paragraph, their words), why (1 paragraph, ASF's words), quote {text, who}, funding (what they have accomplished during the partnership, 1 paragraph), numbers (list of {value, label}), donate, contact, photo (path relative to the partner's folder, or empty).

partners.name: Black E.S.T.E.E.M.
partners.tagline: Hands-on STEM, leadership, and entrepreneurship programs building confidence and career pathways for Black girls ages 8–16 across the GTA.
partners.serves: Black girls ages 8–16 across the Greater Toronto Area
offers: Hands-on STEM workshops and camps
Leadership and mentorship programs
Entrepreneurship training for teens
Exposure to Black women in science, technology, engineering, and business
partners.what: Black E.S.T.E.E.M. (Entrepreneurs, Scientists, Technicians, Engineers, Economists, Mathematicians) runs hands-on programs where Black girls build, code, experiment, pitch, and lead. The organization started as a founder-led grassroots effort and has grown into a GTA-wide program with workshops, camps, and a network of mentors drawn from the fields the girls are being introduced to.
partners.why: Black E.S.T.E.E.M. reminded one of our advisors of the community mentorship that opened doors in her own youth: deeply rooted, focused on access, opportunity, and long-term economic mobility, with a clear vision and real partnerships. The organization has grown from 50 girls to a network of more than 500 on a modest budget and no full-time staff. For a group at this stage, we believe five years of unrestricted money is not a supplement but a transformation, the shift from program-funded to organization-funded.

partners.name: MIND Program
partners.tagline: Moving In New Directions delivers free homemade meals and on-site food banks to Toronto Community Housing residents in Scarborough facing food insecurity.
partners.serves: Toronto Community Housing residents in Scarborough facing food insecurity
offers: Free homemade meals delivered to community housing sites
On-site food banks
Partnerships with frontline agencies already working in each building
partners.what: MIND Program (Moving In New Directions) brings food to where people already are. Working through frontline organizations in Toronto Community Housing buildings in Scarborough, MIND delivers free homemade meals and runs on-site food banks for residents who cannot easily get to a food bank across the city. The meals are cooked, not pre-packaged, and the program is built around the dignity of the people receiving them.
partners.why: MIND has a model we had not seen elsewhere: partnering with frontline health and harm-reduction agencies that cannot provide food themselves, and bringing homemade, culturally appropriate meals to where people already are. Meals at one harm-reduction hub tripled the number of people seeking its services. MIND had just earned a Toronto Foundation grant and a place in its Good to Give Guide, and its director had deliberately kept the organization from "chasing the same piece of pie." Our decision was unanimous.

partners.name: Oasis Youth Care Programs
partners.tagline: Transitional housing and wrap-around support helping Black and racialized youth in Halton and Peel move from homelessness to stable, permanent homes.
partners.serves: Black and racialized youth experiencing homelessness in Halton and Peel Regions
offers: Oasis House transitional homes in Oakville
A resource centre for youth not in residence
Case management, life skills, and housing search support
A path to permanent housing, with follow-up after move-out
partners.what: Oasis Youth Care Programs runs transitional homes for young people who have nowhere stable to live, and surrounds that housing with the support it takes to leave it well: case management, life skills, help with school and work, and a housing search that ends in a lease. Oasis is based in Oakville and serves Halton and Peel, suburbs where youth homelessness is real but services are thin.
partners.why: Oasis is meeting an urgent, unmet need: it has had to turn away youth leaving Children's Aid, with 78 referrals over six years against capacity for 21. It is Halton's only intentionally Black-led, Black-serving youth housing program, and 90% of residents move on to permanent housing. One of its two houses was being kept open month to month by individual donors. We weighed the small number of residents against the depth of the need and concluded that few grants in our portfolio would matter more per dollar.

partners.name: Power To Girls Foundation
partners.tagline: School-based mentorship, leadership, and wellness programming that builds sisterhood and self-worth for Black girls and young women across the GTA.
partners.serves: Black girls and young women across the Greater Toronto Area
offers: School-based mentorship circles
Leadership and wellness programming
Annual conferences and summer opportunities
The MY Power app
Youth-led research on the experiences of Black girls in Ontario schools
partners.what: Power To Girls runs mentorship and leadership programs inside schools, where Black girls spend most of their day and where, too often, they are overlooked or over-disciplined. Programs are built around sisterhood: small circles, consistent mentors, and space to be a whole person. The organization also does its own research, including a multi-year study of Black girls' educational experiences across Ontario, and uses it to shape what it offers.
partners.why: Power To Girls has built a mentorship ecosystem for Black girls that is school-based, culturally specific, designed with the girls themselves, and structured so that girls who were mentored come back as mentors. Since 2013 it has reached more than 10,000 girls across the GTA, runs in roughly eleven schools with fifteen more waiting, and did its own research with 245 Black girls on their experience of Ontario schools. We debated scale against depth and concluded that an organization serving 350 girls a year, with funding streams drying up, was exactly where multi-year money should go.

partners.name: Sawubona Africentric Circle of Support
partners.tagline: Culturally responsive caregiver support, workshops, and advocacy for Black families raising children and adults with disabilities.
partners.led_by: Sherron Grant and Clovis Grant, Co-founders
partners.serves: Black families in the GTA raising children and adults with disabilities and special needs
offers: Peer support circles for caregivers
One-to-one help navigating services and funding
Workshops and a caregiver toolkit in English and French
Community events that bring isolated families together
Advocacy within the disability and education systems
partners.what: Sawubona is a Zulu greeting that means "I see you." The organization was founded by parents who found that disability services were not built with Black families in mind, and who wanted a place where families like theirs could be seen. It runs peer support circles, one-to-one navigation support, workshops, and community gatherings, and equips caregivers to advocate for their family members inside systems that are often hard to move.
partners.why: Sawubona fills a gap that remains badly under-served: Black families raising children and adults with disabilities, navigating hard systems with little culturally responsive support. The co-founders are parents of an adult child with special needs and have professionalized the organization while running it as unpaid volunteers, reaching more than 300 caregivers, completing an external evaluation, and writing a five-year plan. We called its impact transformational, and it is the first partner in our history working on disability.

partners.name: Black Creek Community Farm
partners.tagline: An urban agricultural centre rooted in Toronto's Jane and Finch neighbourhood, engaging diverse communities through sustainable food.
partners.serves: Residents of Jane and Finch and surrounding northwest Toronto neighbourhoods
offers: A working farm inside the city
Fresh, affordable produce for the neighbourhood
Youth and community programming on the land
partners.what: Black Creek Community Farm is a working farm in Jane and Finch, one of Toronto's most diverse and least-served neighbourhoods. It grows food for the community, employs and trains local residents and youth, and uses the land as a gathering place for education, culture, and food justice work.
partners.why: In 2021 we saw in Black Creek Community Farm strong, dynamic leadership, a community kitchen we loved, a focus on accessibility, and a range of programs backed by early revenue-generating work. The farm operates through FoodShare as a shared platform, which made us think hard about how we wanted to support grassroots groups working under a charitable mentor, a question that has shaped our approach since. We funded the farm for what it is: a working farm in Jane and Finch, led from within its community.
partners.funding: The farm grew 22,000 pounds of produce in a recent year, distributed through its sliding-scale Harvest Share program and farm stands, and its Urban Harvest partnership with the City redistributed more than 2,900 kg of food to local food banks and programs, reaching nearly 700 households. It has launched a Land Stewardship Program rooted in Indigenous and diasporic knowledge, a Youth Farm Residency for Black, Indigenous, and racialized youth from Jane-Finch, and joined the Nourish Leadership Anchor Cohort on food and health.

partners.name: Community Justice Collective
partners.tagline: Legal support for community organizers and social justice movements across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area.
partners.serves: Community organizers, tenants, and social movements across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area
offers: Legal advice and representation for organizers and movements
Know-your-rights education
Support for tenant and community campaigns
partners.what: Community Justice Collective is a movement lawyering organization. It provides legal support to the organizers, tenant groups, and grassroots campaigns that larger legal clinics cannot take on, and it does so as a partner in the work rather than a service provider at arm's length.
partners.why: When we met Community Justice Collective in 2023, it had three lawyers, a donated office, low salaries, and a client list it had never lost a member of. It provides legal defence for tenant unions, encampment residents, mutual-aid organizers, and land defenders, people whom institutions with money or power try to slow down through the legal process. CJC had already beaten dozens of eviction and encampment charges. It needed money it could direct without anyone telling it whom to represent, and that is what unrestricted funding is for.
partners.funding: CJC has acted as counsel for rent strikes across the city, including a precedent-setting win at 1440–1442 Lawrence Avenue West that reversed an illegal eviction and compelled the landlord to fix the building. It influenced provincial bail-reform legislation, partnered with U of T's Faculty of Law on a legal-tech tool for marginalized communities, mentored 13 aspiring lawyers, and launched Counsel Call, which became Canada's top "How To" podcast. It used part of our grant to pay tenant leaders to become organizers, and is now expanding into workers' rights.

partners.name: Homeless Connect Toronto
partners.tagline: Coordinates "one-stop-shop" events connecting people at risk of or experiencing homelessness with the supports they need.
partners.serves: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness in Toronto
offers: Large one-day service events bringing dozens of providers under one roof
Health care, ID, housing, employment, and legal supports on site
A volunteer base drawn from across the city
partners.what: Homeless Connect Toronto runs events where someone who is homeless or close to it can, in a single day, see a doctor, replace lost ID, talk to a housing worker, get a haircut, and sit down for a meal. The organization's work is bringing the system to the person, once, in one place, instead of asking them to navigate it alone.
partners.why: Homeless Connect Toronto applied in our first round in 2021. We scored it highly but could only choose five. By 2023 it had done what we had hoped: used three years of unrestricted funding from another funder to grow beyond its signature one-stop-shop events into year-round Community Connect events, a peer-connector program run entirely by people with lived experience of homelessness, and an online portal. Its director wanted every person working there to be sustainably employed. We funded that.
partners.funding: Homeless Connect's October 2024 one-stop-shop served a record 1,240 guests with 339 volunteers and 322 service providers from 67 organizations. PeerConnectTO has trained three cohorts of peer workers with lived experience of homelessness, Everyday Connect gives people a 24/7 portal to nearby services, and the organization is part of a St. Michael's study on whether peer support improves health outcomes. It ran matching campaigns around our grant and in 2024 secured $69,337 in new grants alongside $210,000 in renewed commitments.

partners.name: ENAGB Indigenous Youth Agency
partners.tagline: Cultural, employment, life-skills, and wellness programs designed by and for Indigenous youth ages 12–29 in Toronto.
partners.serves: Indigenous youth ages 12–29 in Toronto, and families with children 0–6 through its EarlyON program
offers: Cultural programming and land-based learning
Employment and life-skills training
Holistic wellness and recreation
An EarlyON program for Indigenous families
An annual cultural festival and competition powwow
partners.what: ENAGB — Eshkiniigjik Naandwechigegamig, Aabiish Gaa Binjibaaying: a place for healing our youth; where did we come from? — is an Indigenous-led youth agency in Toronto. Its programs are designed through Indigenous youth participation and are built to grow self-esteem, confidence, skills, and self-determination, with culture at the centre: ceremony, land-based learning, and a Youth Council that shapes what the agency does.
partners.why: When we reviewed ENAGB in 2021 it ranked near the top for all of us, with no reservations. What stood out was how youth-centred it is: at every point, the young people it serves have a real say in how it runs and where it focuses, and much of the work was being carried by volunteers. We saw something rare, an organization that is youth-led as well as youth-serving, and we believed unrestricted funding could help build the infrastructure its growth needed.
partners.funding: ENAGB has opened a West End location and runs land-based learning and ceremony at Memtigwaake Kinomaage Maawnjiding, a 2.7-acre cultural site on the Humber River. It secured $1 million over four years from the MLSE Foundation and a $900,000 commitment from Sun Life for play-based programming, and in 2026 launched a large-scale competition powwow at Woodbine Park. The grassroots agency we met in 2021 is now a city-wide one.

partners.name: Maggie's Toronto Sex Workers Action Project
partners.tagline: Canada's oldest sex-worker justice initiative, offering wrap-around services and life-affirming care across Toronto and the GTA.
partners.serves: Sex workers across Toronto and the GTA
offers: Drop-in and outreach services
Harm reduction supplies and support
Peer-led programming and advocacy
partners.what: Maggie's is run by and for sex workers. It provides harm reduction, drop-in support, outreach, and advocacy grounded in the principle that sex workers are the experts on their own safety and their own lives. It has done this work in Toronto for decades, through changes in law and in public opinion.
partners.why: We were unanimous that Maggie's serves one of the most neglected and vulnerable communities in the city, and does it as a peer-led organization that also supports people who are homeless and advocates for people with the least choice. We liked that Maggie's asked for funding for its own leadership capacity rather than a project. Government funding kept the lights on but left the team overstretched; we believed unrestricted money would relieve real pressure on the people doing the work.
partners.funding: Maggie's unionized in 2021 and, after a 2023 fire caused at least $500,000 in damage to its main office, kept its drop-in, outreach, and harm-reduction work running through major operational changes. It secured $850,000 over five years from the Public Health Agency of Canada.

partners.name: The Reading Partnership
partners.tagline: Builds literacy programs and resources for families and children in the Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park community of Scarborough.
partners.serves: Children and families in Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park, Scarborough
offers: Parent-led early literacy programs
Reading resources and books for the home
Community events built around reading
partners.what: The Reading Partnership works on the belief that parents are a child's first teachers. In Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park, it trains and supports parents to build reading into daily life, puts books into homes, and runs programs that make literacy a community project rather than a school-only one.
partners.why: Camesha Cox told us in 2023 that The Reading Partnership had been chronically underfunded and overlooked for most of its twelve years, running on a shared platform and then a trusteeship before finally becoming an independent charity. The model is prevention: better literacy leads to better outcomes in everything else, and the programs feed families so they can take part. What the organization needed was internal capacity, fundraising, government relations, and program staff, which no project grant would pay for. Ours could.
partners.funding: The Reading Partnership launched its 2024–2027 strategic plan and a research collaboration with the Canadian Children's Literacy Foundation on the reading journeys of Black children in Canada. Camesha Cox was inducted into the Scarborough Walk of Fame and named an Ashoka Fellow. The organization used our grant as a match for its year-end appeal, raising $43,641.91 and finding that supporters gave more because of it, an approach it has since shared with every partner in our cohort.

numbers.label: raised with a matched year-end appeal
TD Ready Challenge grant to scale nationally

partners.name: Toronto Alliance to End Homelessness
partners.tagline: A community-based collective-impact initiative working toward a Toronto where homelessness is rare, brief, and non-recurring.
partners.serves: The homelessness-serving sector in Toronto, and through it, people experiencing homelessness
offers: Coordination across agencies, funders, and government
Data and advocacy for a housing-first system
A platform for people with lived experience to shape policy
partners.what: The Toronto Alliance to End Homelessness brings together the agencies, advocates, and people with lived experience who make up Toronto's homelessness response, and pushes for a system that ends homelessness rather than managing it. Its work is coordination, data, and advocacy, the connective tissue that individual shelters and programs cannot build alone.
partners.why: TAEH is a collective-impact organization: it exists to pull Toronto's homelessness sector out of competition and into coalition, and to move policy from "not in my backyard" to "yes." It is deliberately not funded by the City, because it advises the City. When we met in 2023 the team was small and the ask was for the unglamorous things, communications, web, administration, that let a policy organization do its mission. Its paid caucus of people with lived experience, built into every decision, is the kind of practice we want to fund.
partners.funding: In November 2024 the City procured TAEH, with the Infrastructure Institute, to provide wrap-around support to applicants to the new $15 million Community Housing Pre-Development Fund, helping newer organizations develop rental and supportive housing. TAEH is the formally recognized non-Indigenous Community Advisory Board to the City on housing and homelessness, and its pre-budget submission to the federal government set out specific recommendations on housing funds, refugee settlement, and mental-health funding for homelessness services.

partners.name: Toronto Black Farmers
partners.tagline: A collective of urban farmers and growers building a community food hub focused on food sovereignty, justice, and access to clean food.
partners.serves: Black communities in Toronto seeking access to culturally relevant, clean food
offers: Urban growing sites and a community food hub
Training for new Black farmers and growers
Culturally relevant produce for the community
partners.what: Toronto Black Farmers and Food Growers Collective grows food, trains growers, and builds the infrastructure of a community food hub rooted in Black food traditions. Its work is about sovereignty as much as supply: who owns the land, who grows the food, and who decides what the community eats.
partners.why: We visited the farm twice before deciding, and came away, in one advisor's words, blown away. Here was an organization excellent at the work itself, growing good, locally grown, accessible food and teaching people to grow their own, while struggling to pay for even basic administration. We chose our grant to serve the back end: the expenses a shoestring organization had never been able to afford, so the farming could grow.
partners.funding: Toronto Black Farmers now provides produce year-round at its Downsview Park farm stand and through the summer at the Afro-Caribbean Farmers Market, alongside workshops, hands-on training, and youth farming programs. Jacqueline and Noel remain two of the most outspoken voices for food justice in the city.

partners.name: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society
partners.tagline: Trauma-informed, culturally grounded services and housing for First Nations, Inuit, and Métis 2SLGBTQIA+ women exiting the justice system.
partners.serves: First Nations, Inuit, and Métis women and 2SLGBTQIA+ people leaving the justice system in Toronto
offers: Toronto's first Indigenous women's healing lodge, in development
Culturally grounded, trauma-informed support
Housing and reintegration services
partners.what: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society is building Toronto's first healing lodge for Indigenous women and 2SLGBTQIA+ people leaving prison: a place to live, heal, and reconnect with culture rather than a halfway house. Its services are designed by Indigenous women and grounded in ceremony, community, and the understanding that incarceration is one chapter of a longer story.
partners.why: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society was an enthusiastic yes for us in 2021. The community it serves is highly neglected, Indigenous women are over-represented in the justice system, and too often they leave prison for a shelter. We were struck by the organization's strength, its grounding in Indigenous culture, and its no-nonsense approach. The lodge is a big project and our grant is small beside it, but we judged the work critical enough to be in from the start.
partners.funding: When we first partnered in 2021 the lodge was a plan. The City redirected a three-storey house to the society in February 2022; it opened as a temporary healing lodge that December, added a garden suite in 2024, and building permits for the main lodge were issued in March 2025 with construction under way. Alongside the build, the society runs Daughters of the Earth, a 16-week program for women on probation or bail, and is developing Indigikwe, a social enterprise that will train up to 24 women a year.

partners.name: Wanasah
partners.tagline: A non-profit mental-health agency addressing the urgent needs of Black youth and their families in Regent Park and surrounding downtown Toronto neighbourhoods.
partners.serves: Black youth and their families in Regent Park and surrounding downtown Toronto neighbourhoods
offers: Counselling and therapy by Black clinicians
Family and community support
Culturally responsive care for Black youth
partners.what: Wanasah provides mental-health care for Black youth and families in Regent Park by clinicians who share their background. It was founded on the recognition that the mainstream system was not reaching Black youth in crisis, and that care has to be culturally responsive, close to home, and free of the barriers that keep families from asking for help.
partners.why: Namarig Ahmed grew up in Regent Park and had never seen mental-health services there. When she and co-founder Dr. Leslie Shanks asked every agency in the neighbourhood whether anyone would support Black youth, the answer was no, so they built Wanasah: therapists who look like their clients, an "auntie" on staff, mothers brought in first. Three years in, they knew they had saved lives. They had turned down grants that would pull them off mission. We funded Wanasah so it would not have to.
partners.funding: Wanasah secured what grassroots organizations rarely do: $100,000 in core funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health, following a $400,000 federal investment in Black-centric, trauma-responsive services in Regent Park. It integrated with Unity Health at St. Michael's Hospital, added a counsellor and a trusted psychiatrist to the team, consulted on Toronto Foundation's Vital Signs report, and grew a group of 50 youth ambassadors, several of whom have become staff. In June 2025 Namarig Ahmed received the King Charles III Coronation Medal from the Governor General.
